newsitem.title: UK: Wine lovers lap up Webber's vintages at auction.
newsitem.headline: Wine lovers lap up Webber's vintages at auction.

text.p: Wine lovers from around the world lapped up Andrew Lloyd Webber's collection of prize vintages on Tuesday, bidding far more than had been expected at the first session of a two-day sale.
Sotheby's auction house said the session had raised a total of over 1.3 million pounds ($2.1 million), with 90 percent of the 304 lots selling above the highest estimate.

The most spectacular offering in the sale was the "Millennium Cellar Super Lot", a selection of some of the greatest wines ever produced, which was bought by the wine director of a Las Vegas hotel chain for 242,000 pounds.

"We sell 2,000 bottles of wine a day and we were running out. The wine we have bought tonight is for drinking," said Barrie Larvin of the Rio Hotel Group in Las Vegas after snapping up one imperial, three double magnums, two jeroboams, 77 magnums and 265 bottles.
The two-day auction had been expected to fetch two million pounds ($3.3 million) but it seems clear the total will far exceed that figure.

A case of Chateau Cheval Blanc 1947, described as a "vinous milestone of this century", sold for 35,200 pounds. Three cases of 1947 Chateau Latour a Pomerol, modestly described as "absolutely sensational", each sold for the same amount.

When the Oscar-winning British composer was not writing hit musicals "Evita" and "Cats", he was putting together what Sotheby's describe as "the greatest single-owner wine collection ever to be offered at auction".
An incurable collector, he bought 18,000 bottles, which is more fine wine than anyone could ever drink.
"Wine is alive and now I realise I have been hogging far too much of it. It is time for a clear-out," Lloyd Webber says in the introduction to the sumptuously produced auction catalogue.
Sotheby's describes the cellar as the stuff of every connoisseur's dreams.
"It is a roll call of the most beautiful and perhaps the most opulent wines ever to be created," said Serena Sutcliffe, head of Sotheby's wine department.
Her own personal favourite is the Chateau d'Yquem 1900, expected to fetch up to 3,000 pounds a bottle.
There are also cheaper wines on sale, with cases of good white Burgundy at around 200 pounds.
"That's the kind of thing I'd go for and leave the billionaires to fight it out for the '47s," said Sutcliffe.
Lloyd Webber began his collection when he was at school and is selling some bottles of 1961 claret he bought for as little as one pound.
He has not given up the wine collecting habit. He is back in the market, this time buying young 1995 vintages from France and the New World.
